title: How to Evaluate an Agentic Support Platform: A Simple Checklist | Pylon
summary: Every support tool says it's agentic now. Here's a simple checklist for testing what an AI agent can really see, do, and cost before you buy.
body_markdown:
> **The short version:** Bring your five hardest real tickets to every demo. Then check what the agent knows before it starts, what it can actually do in your tools, where it works, how it hands off to your team, and what it costs when your ticket volume doubles. The best demo isn't the slickest one. It's the one that handles your tickets.


Every support tool calls itself agentic now. The demos all look great.


The hard part is figuring out what happens on a normal Tuesday, with your tickets, your customers, and your messy systems. This is the checklist we'd use if we were buying.


## Start with one real ticket, not a feature list


Before you take any demo, pull five tickets from last month. Pick the ones that took your team the longest.


Maybe it's "Why did our export fail?" from a big account. Or "When was this user removed?" where someone had to dig through logs for half an hour.


Bring those to every demo. Ask the vendor to walk through them live. You'll learn more in 20 minutes than from any slide.


## Question 1: What does the agent know before it starts?


A chatbot starts with your help center. An agent should start with the customer.


Ask what the agent can see on a new ticket. Good answers sound like this:


- Who the customer is, what plan they're on, and how they use the product
- What they said in past tickets, emails, and calls
- Whether you've seen this issue before and how you fixed it
- Any open bugs or feature requests that might be related


If the answer is "it reads your knowledge base," that's a chatbot with a new name. That's fine for simple questions. It won't help much with the hard ones.


## Question 2: Can it actually do things?


Answering is the easy part. The real time sink is the work around the answer.


Ask the vendor to show the agent doing things in your other tools:


- Checking logs or account data
- Filing a bug with the right details
- Updating a field in your CRM
- Routing the ticket to the right team
- Giving a heads up to the account owner


Then ask the follow-up: can you control what it's allowed to do? You want to pick which actions need a human to approve first. "It can do anything" is not a feature.


## Question 3: Does it work where your customers already are?


If you support businesses, a lot of your customers probably aren't using a chat bubble on your website.


They're in a shared Slack channel. Or Microsoft Teams. Or email, with three people from their team on the thread.


Ask which channels the agent works in today. Then ask if it's the same agent in every channel, with the same context, or a separate bot for each one.


(If most of your customers live in shared channels, we wrote more about that in[Slack-first support for B2B teams](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/slack-first-b2b-support) .)


## Question 4: What happens when it hands off to a person?


Every agent will hit something it can't solve. That's normal. What matters is what your team gets when it does.


The bad version: a ticket that says "Customer needs help," and your engineer starts from zero.


The good version: a short summary of what the customer asked, what the agent checked, what it found, and what it suggests doing next. Your person picks it up in two minutes instead of thirty.


Ask to see a real handoff. Not a mockup.


## Question 5: Can your team change how it works?


Your product changes every week. Your support process changes with it.


So ask who can update the agent's instructions. If every tweak needs an engineer, or a ticket to the vendor, it'll fall behind fast.


The best setups let the people closest to the work write instructions in everyday language and share them with the whole team. Ask to see someone edit one live.


## Question 6: Can you test it before it talks to customers?


You wouldn't ship code without testing it. Same goes here.


Ask if you can run the agent on past tickets and see what it would have said. Ask if you can try a change on a small slice of tickets before turning it on for everyone.


If the only way to test is "turn it on and watch," that's a risk you're taking on.


## Question 7: How does the price grow with you?


This one gets skipped in a lot of demos. Don't skip it.


Pricing usually falls into a few buckets:


- **Per resolution.** You pay each time the AI closes a ticket.
- **Per conversation.** You pay for every chat, solved or not.
- **Per seat.** You pay for each person on the team.
- **Usage credits.** You buy a pool of credits that agent work draws from.


None of these is wrong. But do the math with your real numbers.


Take your monthly ticket volume. Now double it, because that's where you hope to be. What does the bill look like then? If the cost climbs every time a customer writes in, a busy month gets expensive fast.


## Question 8: Can you trust it with customer data?


Agents touch a lot of sensitive stuff. Ask the boring questions early.


- Do they have SOC 2 Type II?
- Where is your data stored? Can you keep it in the EU if you need to?
- Is there an audit log of what the agent did?
- Can you limit which systems and records the agent can see?


If a vendor gets vague here, that tells you something.


## Question 9: Does it help anyone besides support?


Here's one people forget. The same context that helps support is useful to everyone else, too.


Sales wants to know what's going on with an account before a call. Customer success wants to spot a renewal at risk. Product wants to know which bugs keep coming up.


Ask if those teams can ask the agent questions too, ideally in a tool they already use, like Slack. If the answer is yes, the value goes way beyond your ticket queue.


## A quick scorecard you can steal


Score each vendor from 1 to 5 on each question, using your five real tickets.


Question What a 5 looks like


Context Knows the account, history, and related bugs before it starts


Actions Does real work in your tools, with approval controls you set


Channels Same agent across Slack, Teams, email, chat, and more


Handoff Hands your team a summary, what it checked, and a next step


Editing Your support team can update instructions in everyday language


Testing You can run it on past tickets before going live


Pricing Cost stays predictable as ticket volume grows


Security SOC 2 Type II, data residency options, audit logs, scoped access


Reach Other teams can use the same context, not just support


Add it up. The highest score with your tickets wins, not the slickest demo.

## FAQ


### What's the most important thing to test in an agentic support platform?


Test it on your own hardest tickets. Watch what the agent knows before it starts, what it can actually do, and what your team gets when it hands off.


### How is an agentic support platform different from a chatbot?


A chatbot answers questions, usually from your help center. An agentic platform uses customer context and connected tools to investigate and take action, then brings in a person when judgment is needed.


### Should an AI support agent run fully on its own?


Not on day one. Most teams start with the agent investigating and drafting while a person reviews. As trust grows, they let it handle more on its own, one workflow at a time.


### How should I compare pricing between vendors?


Model your real ticket volume, then double it. Compare what each pricing model costs at both numbers. Per-resolution and per-conversation pricing grow with volume. Seats and credits tend to be easier to predict.


### How long should an evaluation take?


A few weeks is usually enough. Run each vendor on the same set of real tickets so you're comparing apples to apples.

### Should an agentic support platform replace my help desk or plug into it?


Ask each vendor. Some AI agents plug into the help desk you already run, so you pay for and maintain two systems and the account context is split between them.
